hazards.damaged-cable: That cable has a cut through to the screen. A damaged DC lead on a 350 kW charger is not a cosmetic fault; bin it and tag the unit out of service.
hazards.dc-busbar: That is the DC link busbar. The supply being open means nothing here — the capacitors hold hundreds of volts for minutes after shutdown, and they will not let go once you are across them.
hazards.interlock-bypass: That jumper defeats the door interlock. Every bypass ever fitted 'just for testing' is still fitted. The interlock is the last thing standing between the next technician and the DC link.
hazards.live-connector: The vehicle is still in a charging session. Pulling a CCS connector under load draws a DC arc that will not self-extinguish — stop the session at the vehicle or the charger first.

interrupts.alert: A car has come round the cones and nosed into the bay behind you. The driver is out, the barrier is shoved over against the kerb and he is looking for the other gun.
interrupts.cue: You are stood still at a timer for ten minutes. That is the whole window.
interrupts.missNote: The bay stayed open with a car and a member of the public inside it. The service door is swung wide onto the module stack, the DC link sits behind a guard anybody can lift, and the only thing keeping a stranger out of it was luck.
interrupts.why: A charge point is not a plant room; it is a parking space on a forecourt with a queue behind it, and the people in that queue have no idea what a technician standing still for ten minutes is doing. The discharge wait is the longest stretch of this job where nothing appears to be happening, which makes it the stretch in which the work zone gets taken apart by strangers. The zone goes back up before anything else, because what comes next is a cabinet open onto an eight-hundred-volt link at about the height of a child.
interrupts.wrongNote: It is the barrier. The work zone is what makes the rest of this procedure safe, and somebody has just taken it apart.

interrupts.alert: Over at the supply pillar your padlock is lying on the top cap and the feeder handle has been swung part of the way back. The site's duty electrician is stood at it chasing a trip on the next bay.
interrupts.cue: You have a module in your hands and somebody else has your isolation.
interrupts.missNote: The handle went the rest of the way over with the guard off and a module out of the stack. Four hundred volts came back into a cabinet that had a person inside it, and the first anybody knew about it was the unit booting.
interrupts.why: A lock is a claim on a piece of equipment, and it only works if the person who finds it can read whose it is and get hold of them. Feeder pillars on retail sites are shared between the chargers, the lighting and the wash, and a tag gone soft in the rain is a tag nobody will honour at seven in the evening with a queue building. Get the handle back over to OFF first: the argument about the lock can wait, because the handle is the part that decides whether the busbar in front of you is live.
interrupts.wrongNote: The handle is the thing that has moved. Put the isolation back where you left it before you deal with anything else on that pillar.

lateNotes.power-module: The module comes out after the link is proven dead, not before.
lateNotes.torque-wrench: Nothing gets torqued while there is stored energy behind the panel.

name: Charge Point

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Open the job on the tablet: fault code, unit history, isolation plan.
steps.prompt: Open the job on the tablet: fault code, unit history, isolation plan.
steps.title: Read the work order and fault code
steps.why: The fault code identifies which power module tripped and which feeder point supplies it — a dual-head 350 kW unit has two isolation points on one pad. Walk up and start opening doors without reading it first and you isolate the healthy bay while the faulted one, busbar included, stays live behind the next panel you touch.

steps.cue: Stop the session at the vehicle side before touching anything.
steps.prompt: Stop the session at the vehicle side before touching anything.
steps.title: End the charging session
steps.why: A controlled stop ramps the charging current down to zero over several seconds and releases the connector latch; every step after this assumes the cable is carrying no load. Pull the plug at the vehicle before the session ends and you snap a live DC connection apart under full current instead of an open one.

steps.cue: Close the bay: two cones and the barrier.
steps.prompt: Close the bay: two cones and the barrier.
steps.title: Establish the work zone
steps.why: A charging bay sits in a live traffic lane on a forecourt that never closes for your job. The cones and barrier tell a driver pulling in for the next bay that this one is occupied by a person, not an idle charger, while your head and hands are inside an open cabinet door.

steps.cue: Take the insulating gloves and shield from the case.
steps.prompt: Take the insulating gloves and shield from the case.
steps.title: Don class 0 gloves and face shield
steps.why: Class 0 rubber gloves rated to 1,000 V, worn under leather protectors, plus a face shield, go on before the door opens, not after the meter reads clear. The DC link behind that guard does not care that the upstream AC supply is off — it stays a stored-energy hazard until it is proven dead, and the glove class is chosen for that voltage.

steps.cue: Swing the feeder disconnect handle on the supply pillar all the way down to OFF.
steps.prompt: Swing the feeder disconnect handle on the supply pillar all the way down to OFF.
steps.title: Open the upstream AC disconnect
steps.why: Isolate at the source feeder, not at the charger's own contactor — a control-level stop is software, not an isolation, and OSHA's 29 CFR 1910.333 electrical safe-work-practice rule requires the equipment be placed in an electrically safe condition before anyone works on it. The handle has to swing fully over; a disconnect blade left partway across the gap is still close enough to strike an arc if it is bumped.

steps.cue: Apply your padlock and tag to the disconnect handle.
steps.prompt: Apply your padlock and tag to the disconnect handle.
steps.title: Lock and tag the disconnect
steps.why: Your lock, your key, your tag with your name on it — the disconnect stays open only as long as nobody else has a reason to believe it's clear to close. A charger that comes back to life while your hands are inside the module bay is a charger someone else re-energised because there was nothing on that handle telling them not to.

steps.cue: Hold at the discharge timer for the full manufacturer wait.
steps.holdBreakNote: You broke the wait. The capacitors are still holding charge — start the full discharge period again.
steps.prompt: Hold at the discharge timer for the full manufacturer wait.
steps.title: Wait out the DC link discharge
steps.why: The bleed resistors need the manufacturer's full stated time to pull the link capacitors down from hundreds of volts to a safe residual; the discharge curve is not linear, and the last dangerous fraction of it lingers after most of the voltage looks gone. Counting to ten and cracking the panel early is how a technician learns, once, exactly what a charged DC link feels like across two fingers.

steps.cue: Meter across the DC link and commit when the reading is safe.

gauge.label: DC LINK — TERMINAL VOLTAGE
gauge.missNote: Still holding charge. Leave the leads on and let it bleed down — do not open the guard at that voltage.

steps.prompt: Meter across the DC link and commit when the reading is safe.
steps.title: Prove the DC link is dead
steps.why: Absence of voltage is measured with a CAT IV meter, never assumed from a timer running out — a bleed resistor can fail open and leave the link fully charged with no outward sign of it. The reading has to sit below the manufacturer's safe threshold before the guard comes off; anything higher means the discharge circuit didn't finish its job.

steps.cue: Slide the failed module out of the stack and set it on the module cart.

drag.missNote: Not on the cart — a failed module put down anywhere else is a module that ends up back in a charger.

steps.prompt: Slide the failed module out of the stack and set it on the module cart.
steps.title: Withdraw the faulty power module
steps.why: Modules are hot-swap rated in service, not in fault. With the link proven dead you can handle it without the arc risk. It goes straight onto the cart, because a module left on the ground gets stepped on and one left in the van gets fitted to the next job.

steps.cue: Set the wrench and torque the busbar bolt to specification.

gauge.label: BUSBAR TORQUE
gauge.missNote: Off specification. A joint outside the torque window is a future thermal fault — reset and take it again.

steps.prompt: Set the wrench and torque the busbar bolt to specification.
steps.title: Torque the busbar connection
steps.why: Under-torqued busbar bolts leave a high-resistance joint that runs hot under load, loosens further and eventually arcs or welds itself together; over-torqued ones crack the lug or strip the thread and fail from the other direction. The number on the manufacturer's label is the number — not a starting point to feel for by hand.

steps.cue: Remove the lock, re-energise and run a commissioning session.
steps.prompt: Remove the lock, re-energise and run a commissioning session.
steps.title: Restore and test-charge
steps.why: The job is not finished at the bolted joint. A test session under real load is what actually proves the fix — a module can look seated and torqued correctly and still fault the instant current flows through it, and the only way to find that out is on your shift, not the next customer's.
